topic: Fan death (선풍기 사망설): Korean belief that sleeping in a closed room with an electric fan on can kill; 1927 Jungoe Ilbo article claimed fans create a vacuum and starve lungs of oxygen; 2006 KCPB alert listed asphyxiation from fans/AC among five most common summer accidents (20 CISS cases 2003-05), advised timers, rotation, open doors; science: fans don't change O2/CO2 and can't cause hypothermia; real risk is heat/dehydration in a hot closed room; 1970s energy-saving propaganda theory contradicted by 1927 date
title: In Korea, a Fan Could Kill You in Your Sleep

slides.headline: In Korea, a fan **could kill you in your sleep.**
slides.note: At least, that's what generations grew up hearing.

slides.headline: The **belief**
slides.body: Fall asleep in a closed room with an electric fan running, and you might not wake up. Koreans call it "fan death."

slides.headline: How it **"works"**
slides.body: The story says the fan uses up the oxygen in the room, or chills your body all night until it gives out.

slides.headline: Leave a **door open**
slides.body: So families learned the rules: crack a door or window, and never point the fan straight at a sleeping face.

slides.headline: Set the **timer**
slides.body: Many Koreans set the fan's off-timer before bed, so it shuts down after they fall asleep.

slides.headline: Even **officials** warned
slides.body: In 2006, Korea's consumer protection agency listed suffocation from fans and air conditioners among the five most common summer accidents.

slides.headline: What science **says**
slides.body: A fan doesn't use up oxygen, and its breeze can't chill a body to a deadly temperature. Experts say deaths blamed on fans were heart attacks or strokes.

slides.headline: The **first warning** in print
slides.body: A Korean newspaper claimed fans create a vacuum that starves your lungs. The fear is almost 100 years old.

slides.headline: The **real** risk
slides.body: In a very hot, closed room, a fan only pushes hot air around and dries the body out. That part is a real danger in a heat wave.

slides.headline: Korea, explained **by a Korean.**
slides.body: Follow for the context behind the things Korea does.
slides.graphic: A dim Korean bedroom with an electric fan, blurred behind the text.
slides.design_note: Use the account's established CTA treatment and amber highlight.

caption:
Many Koreans grew up being told never to sleep in a closed room with the fan on. It might kill you.

Science says it won't. But plenty of families still leave the door cracked, just in case.

Did you grow up with a warning like this?
reply: Some say the government made it up in the 1970s to save electricity. That theory doesn't hold up: a Korean newspaper was already warning about fans in 1927.
fact_check: 1·2장: 선풍기 사망설 = 밀폐된 방에서 선풍기 켜고 자면 죽는다는 속설(en·ko 위키 Fan death / 선풍기 사망설).
3장: 산소 결핍·저체온 주장(en 위키, 2006 소비자보호원 문구).
4장: 문 열어두기·얼굴에 직접 바람 금지 = 소비자보호원 2006 권고(문 열기·회전·타이머) + 일반 관행.
5장: 타이머 = 2006 소비자보호원 권고. '많은 한국인' 사용은 일반 관행, 비율 통계 없음.
6장: 한국소비자보호원 2006-07-18 '여름철 안전사고 주의' — 선풍기·에어컨 질식을 5대 여름 사고에 포함, 2003~2005 CISS 20건(en 위키 인용).
7장: 선풍기는 O2·CO2 농도 영향 없음, 저체온 불가(Giesbrecht·서울대병원 정성구, ko 위키 2008 기사 인용). 사인은 심장마비·뇌졸중·호흡부전(Kalkstein).
8장: 1927-07-31 중외일보 '선풍기의 괴이한 해' — 진공·산소 부족 주장(en 위키, 원문 직접 확인 못 함).
9장: 덥고 밀폐된 방에선 해롭다(Kalkstein, ko 위키). WHO 35도 기준은 확인 못 해서 숫자 뺌.
reply: 1970년대 에너지 절약 선전설은 1927 기사로 반박(en 위키, Slate).
